hero.introParagraph: TeleDirectMD treats pediatric ringworm (tinea corporis, ICD-10 B35.4) by secure video visit for children ages 5 to 17. TeleDirectMD is a physician-owned, MD-only telehealth practice operating in 41 states plus Washington, DC, and no nurse practitioners or physician assistants treat children here. A parent or legal guardian must be present and provide consent for every visit. TeleDirectMD treats body ringworm with topical antifungals only; scalp ringworm (tinea capitis) requires oral antifungal therapy and is referred for in-person evaluation. Self-pay visits are $79, and TeleDirectMD does not prescribe controlled substances.

telehealthRegulations.sectionTitle: Telehealth Regulations Across Our Licensed States
paragraphs: TeleDirectMD operates only where its physicians hold active licensure, currently 41 states plus Washington, DC. Each state sets its own telemedicine standards, and in every state a parent or legal guardian must consent to a minor's care. TeleDirectMD verifies that the child is physically located in a licensed state at the time of the visit; care is not provided to children outside the licensed footprint.

Some states require an in-person evaluation before prescribing prescription-strength antifungals for pediatric tinea by telehealth. State-specific pages cite the controlling state statute. TeleDirectMD does not prescribe controlled substances.

paragraphs: Ringworm (tinea corporis) is a common superficial fungal skin infection caused by dermatophyte fungi, not a worm. It produces a ring-shaped, scaly, often itchy patch with a raised border and central clearing.

Ringworm is contagious and common in school-age children, athletes, and pet owners, and responds well to topical antifungals. Per the CDC ringworm clinical overview, topical therapy is adequate for tinea corporis (body ringworm), while scalp ringworm (tinea capitis) requires oral antifungal therapy.

TeleDirectMD focuses on body ringworm in children ages 5 to 17 that can be confirmed by video exam, with a parent present, and refers scalp ringworm, nail fungus, and widespread or non-responding cases to in-person care.

causesAndRiskFactors.sectionTitle: Causes and Risk Factors in Children
causesAndRiskFactors.intro: Pediatric ringworm in children ages 5 to 17 has several recognized causes and contributors:

items.label: Dermatophyte fungi:
items.text: Trichophyton and Microsporum species cause tinea corporis.

items.label: Skin-to-skin contact:
items.text: contact with an infected person or animal (cats and dogs) spreads the fungus.

items.label: Sharing items:
items.text: sharing towels, sports gear, or mats spreads ringworm, which is common among wrestlers.

items.label: Warm, moist skin:
items.text: sweating and warm, moist skin favor fungal growth.

items.label: Contaminated surfaces:
items.text: contact with contaminated surfaces in locker rooms can transmit the fungus.

causesAndRiskFactors.closing: Not every ring-shaped rash is ringworm. Nummular eczema, granuloma annulare, pityriasis rosea, and psoriasis can mimic tinea corporis. TeleDirectMD uses history and video exam to confirm the characteristic ring before recommending treatment and directs atypical presentations to in-person evaluation.

compareCards.title: Ringworm vs Nummular Eczema and Granuloma Annulare
compareCards.text: Tinea corporis is an annular scaly plaque with a raised border and central clearing. Nummular eczema produces coin-shaped itchy patches without the central clearing, and granuloma annulare forms a ring of firm bumps with no scale and little itch. The raised, scaly, advancing border with central clearing is the most reliable clue for ringworm.

compareCards.title: Ringworm vs Pityriasis Rosea, Psoriasis, and Tinea Capitis
compareCards.text: Pityriasis rosea starts with a herald patch followed by a 'Christmas-tree' trunk rash. Psoriasis shows thick silvery plaques, usually on extensor surfaces. Tinea capitis causes scalp scaling and hair loss and, unlike body ringworm, requires oral antifungal therapy, so TeleDirectMD refers it for in-person care.

differentialDiagnosis.closing: If the rash involves the scalp or nails, is widespread, or does not respond to topical antifungal treatment, TeleDirectMD will direct you to in-person care for possible oral therapy and testing.

treatmentOptions.intro: Most body ringworm clears with an over-the-counter or prescription topical antifungal applied for 2 to 4 weeks, continued about a week after the rash clears. A TeleDirectMD physician confirms the appearance by video and selects an appropriate topical agent. Scalp ringworm and nail fungus require oral therapy and are referred for in-person care.

sections.title: First-line topical antifungals
sections.text: Over-the-counter clotrimazole 1% or miconazole 2% cream is first-line for body ringworm and is safe at all pediatric ages. Apply to the patch and about 2 centimeters beyond its border, once or twice daily as directed, for 2 to 4 weeks.

sections.title: Prescription topical options
sections.text: Terbinafine 1% cream (labeled ages 12+, commonly used in younger children) offers an effective, shorter course, and ketoconazole 2% cream (labeled ages 12+) is an alternative. These are used for body ringworm only, not scalp or nail involvement.

sections.title: Duration and relapse prevention
sections.text: Continue treatment for 1 to 2 weeks after the rash looks clear to prevent relapse. Lesions that do not improve in 2 to 4 weeks warrant in-person evaluation and possible testing.

sections.title: What we refer out
sections.text: Scalp ringworm (tinea capitis) and nail fungus require oral antifungal therapy with appropriate monitoring and are referred for in-person evaluation, since topical creams alone do not cure them.

homeCare.sectionTitle: Home Care, Recovery Timeline, Prevention, and Follow-up

whatToDoNow.title: Timeline and What to Do Now
items: Apply the antifungal cream to the patch and about 2 cm beyond the border, once or twice daily as directed.
Continue treatment for 1 to 2 weeks after the rash looks clear to prevent relapse.
Keep skin clean and dry, and change out of sweaty clothes promptly.
Cover lesions during sports and avoid skin-to-skin contact until treatment has started.

whatToWatch.title: What to Watch For During Treatment
items: If lesions do not improve in 2 to 4 weeks, seek in-person evaluation and possible testing.
If scaly bald patches appear on the scalp, this suggests tinea capitis and needs oral therapy.
If lesions spread widely or rapidly, seek in-person care.
Follow up by video if the rash is not clearing as expected.

followUp.title: Prevention and Follow-up
items: Do not share towels, clothing, or sports gear, and wash them in hot water.
Treat infected pets (a common source) with a veterinarian's help.
Keep skin dry and avoid prolonged moisture in skin folds.
Continue treatment for the full directed course even after the rash clears.
Follow up if lesions persist after a full topical course or if scalp or nail involvement develops.

items.question: Can TeleDirectMD treat my child's ringworm online?
items.answer: Yes, for body ringworm. TeleDirectMD treats tinea corporis (ringworm, ICD-10 B35.4) by video for children ages 5 to 17 with a parent present. An MD confirms the ring-shaped rash and prescribes a topical antifungal. The self-pay visit is $79, available in 41 states plus Washington, DC. Scalp ringworm (tinea capitis) requires oral antifungal therapy and is referred for in-person care.

items.question: What does ringworm look like in children?
items.answer: Ringworm appears as a ring-shaped, scaly patch with a raised, advancing border and central clearing, and it is often itchy. Despite the name, it is a fungal infection, not a worm. A TeleDirectMD physician diagnoses tinea corporis by video for children ages 5 to 17 from this characteristic appearance, distinguishing it from eczema, which lacks the clearing center and raised ring.

items.question: What antifungal does TeleDirectMD prescribe for pediatric ringworm?
items.answer: For body ringworm in children ages 5 to 17, TeleDirectMD recommends or prescribes topical antifungals such as clotrimazole 1% or miconazole 2% (both over-the-counter, all ages) first-line, or terbinafine 1% and ketoconazole 2% creams. Treatment continues for one to two weeks after the rash clears to prevent relapse. Topical therapy is sufficient for most body ringworm.

items.question: Why won't TeleDirectMD treat scalp ringworm online?
items.answer: Because scalp ringworm (tinea capitis) requires oral antifungal therapy, which needs in-person evaluation and monitoring beyond a single video visit. TeleDirectMD treats only body ringworm (tinea corporis) for children ages 5 to 17 with topical antifungals. A child with scaly bald patches or scaling on the scalp is referred for in-person assessment, since topical creams alone do not cure tinea capitis.

items.question: Is ringworm contagious, and can my child go to school?
items.answer: Yes, ringworm is contagious through skin-to-skin contact and shared items, and pets are a common source. Children ages 5 to 17 with body ringworm can usually attend school once treatment has started and lesions are covered. TeleDirectMD counsels families not to share towels or sports gear, to wash items in hot water, and to treat infected pets with a veterinarian's help.

items.question: Does a parent need to be present for a ringworm visit?
items.answer: Yes. A parent or legal guardian must be present for the entire visit and provide consent for any child ages 5 to 17 seen by TeleDirectMD for ringworm. The guardian's identity is verified, and the child must be physically located in one of the 41 states plus Washington, DC where TeleDirectMD is licensed at the time of the video visit.

items.question: How long does ringworm take to clear with treatment?
items.answer: Most body ringworm clears with two to four weeks of a topical antifungal, continued about a week after the rash looks clear to prevent relapse. TeleDirectMD advises parents of children ages 5 to 17 to apply the cream to the patch and about two centimeters beyond its border. Lesions that do not improve in two to four weeks warrant in-person evaluation.

items.question: How much does an online pediatric ringworm visit cost?
items.answer: An online pediatric ringworm visit at TeleDirectMD costs $79 self-pay, no insurance required, for children ages 5 to 17. TeleDirectMD is in-network with Aetna, select Blue Cross Blue Shield plans, and UnitedHealthcare where applicable, but is not in-network with any Medicaid, Managed Medicaid, CHIP, or Medicare-Medicaid plan in any state. Many antifungal creams are inexpensive over-the-counter purchases.

items.question: Can ringworm be confused with other rashes?
items.answer: Yes. Ringworm can resemble nummular eczema, granuloma annulare, pityriasis rosea, or psoriasis, which is why a TeleDirectMD physician evaluates the rash by video for children ages 5 to 17. The classic clue is a ring-shaped scaly border with central clearing. If the appearance is atypical or does not respond to antifungal treatment, in-person evaluation and possible testing are recommended.

items.question: Does TeleDirectMD treat ringworm in children under 5?
items.answer: No. TeleDirectMD treats body ringworm only for children ages 5 to 17. Although topical antifungals are safe for younger children, TeleDirectMD's pediatric skin services begin at age 5. Children under 5 with a suspected fungal rash should be evaluated by their pediatrician in person, who can confirm the diagnosis and rule out scalp involvement that would need oral therapy.

paragraphs: This page is informational and is not a substitute for in-person medical care. TeleDirectMD treats children ages 5 to 17 for body ringworm; we do not treat children under age 5 for any condition (ages 0 to 4 are excluded). A parent or legal guardian must be present for the entire visit and provide consent, and the child must be physically located in a licensed state (41 states plus Washington, DC) at the time of the visit.

TeleDirectMD does not prescribe controlled substances or isotretinoin, does not diagnose or treat mental health conditions or ADHD, and does not make new asthma diagnoses. Scalp ringworm (tinea capitis) and nail fungus require oral antifungal therapy and are referred for in-person care. Any infant under 3 months with fever requires emergency care. TeleDirectMD is not in-network with any Medicaid, Managed Medicaid, CHIP, or Medicare-Medicaid plan in any state.
